Custom monomers & conjugates

Define a monomer once and it becomes two things: a button under More monomers, and a code you can type. Codes longer than one letter go in brackets, like (psU). Definitions are kept in this browser, and while you are signed in they sync to your account. The account copy is the one that follows you to another device.

Rows marked working range land between 500 and 2000 m/z, which is what most ESI instruments are set to collect. Oligos ionise in negative mode, meaning they lose protons from the backbone rather than gain them. Which peak comes out tallest depends on your instrument and how it is tuned.

Out of scans before the month is up?
A pack of 50 photo scans is $5, bought once. Not a subscription. The credits never expire, and your monthly scans still reset on their own.

Pooled scans are deliberate. A lab of five gets 100 scans a month from one pool, so the person running a screen is not rationed by the person who scanned nothing that week.

You never lose a strand by downgrading. A quota only stops new saves. Everything already in your library stays readable, exportable and editable on any plan, forever.

Academic labs get 40% off. Ask for a code. That is what the box above is for.

How lab plans work

The question everyone asks first: if my PI buys a lab plan, what happens to my account?

1Your PI pre-authorizes your email address. They add the exact address to the lab roster. There is no joining by university domain, because one university domain covers tens of thousands of people, not your lab. Naming one address is a deliberate act, which is the point.
2You open Oligo MW and sign in with that address. Same email, same 6-digit code, same box. The lab seat attaches itself the first time you sign in. We do not send you an invitation email, so nothing to wait for and nothing to lose in a spam folder. There is no separate lab login and no lab URL to remember.
3You keep your own account. Joining a lab adds a shared library. It does not take over your personal one. Your own strands stay yours, including if you leave the lab.
4The lab pays, not you. If your lab covers you, we say so and grey out the Pro button instead of quietly taking a second payment.

How the molecular weight is built

The average molecular weight is a plain sum. Nothing is hidden in it:

MW = Σ free nucleosides + (n − 1) backbone bridges + 5′/3′ groups (+ custom monomers)

For ATCGATCGAT (10 nt · DNA · all-PO · 5′-OH / 3′-OH): Σ free nucleosides 2,469.36 + 9 × PO bridge 557.68 + terminal 0.00 = 3,027.04 g/mol. Those are the same figures the result panel shows.

Phosphorothioate adds +16.06 g/mol per bond. Monoisotopic mass needs an elemental formula for every unit; ε₂₆₀ uses the nearest-neighbour model.

Method mirrors the production calculator; figures are the real values for this strand.

Writing a sequence

Type 5′→3′. The bases are A C G T U. DNA uses T, RNA uses U, and a U typed while the backbone is DNA is counted as T. Spaces are ignored.

Sugar & 2′-modifications go in front of the base: d/r (DNA/RNA sugar, required in Hybrid mode), m 2′-OMe, f 2′-F, moe 2′-MOE, cEt. For example mA, fG, moeC, cEtA.

One thing to watch with C and U. moeC and moeU are the 5-methyl forms (so moeU is MOE-T), which is what vendors normally ship. cEtC and cEtU are not methylated. If you ordered cEt-5-methyl-C, add the methyl yourself, or define it once as a custom monomer: each one is 14.03 g/mol heavier than what cEtC gives you.

Phosphorothioate, a sulfur backbone link. Put s between two bases: AsTsCsG. Without it the link is a normal phosphodiester (PO).

Custom monomers from the catalog go in brackets, like (GalNAc). Single-letter modifier keys stay bare.

End groups (5′-phosphate, 5′-DMT, 3′-phosphate, inverted-dT…) are set with the end-group controls; the locked affixes they add can’t be deleted from the field.
